prize_parts.citation: For a visionary Romanian oeuvre, from the early poetry to the Blinding trilogy and Solenoid, in which memory, the body and dream are given the form of densely patterned, encyclopedic metaphysical prose.

statement.case_for: My laureate is unchanged, but I hold the choice less firmly than in round 1. I apply one standard to every shortlisted writer. Sustained quality means a recognisable voice that keeps developing and does not fall back on its own devices. Depth of imaginative purpose is how I read the 'ideal direction' of Nobel's will, and I treat it as a test of seriousness, not of subject matter or genre. On that standard, Cărtărescu's strongest claim is a single obsessive project that runs from the poetry into the Blinding trilogy and Solenoid. Memory, the body and dream are not themes laid over a plot. They are built into the structure and the sentences. The project has a scale and continuity of voice that I do not find elsewhere on the shortlist. I read the digressions as the work's method, an accumulating inner cosmos, and I do not read them as a failure of control. I hold that as a judgment from public knowledge and translations, not as something I have verified in Romanian. The citation leads with the poetry, as the foundation of the prose, and does not rest on one large book.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is unchanged and is now sharper. The case depends on sentence-level density, rhythm and syntax in Romanian, which I can judge only through translation and secondary reading, and on a few very large works. Maximalism can turn into repetition. The chair asked what evidence beyond translation and reception would settle the question of economy and control. I do not have it, and I should not claim it. The question can only be settled by reading specific late volumes closely against the earlier ones. If that reading showed repetition and not development, the case would weaken considerably. Anne Carson's case is also stronger than I allowed in round 1. Swärd's anchoring of the citation in original books answers much of my authorship worry, and a citation of that kind is workable. What remains for me is the possibility of mannerism in later work and the dependence on book design. I weigh these as risks, not as defects established against her.

responses.point: Swärd would anchor the Carson citation in original works (Eros the Bittersweet, Autobiography of Red, Plainwater, The Beauty of the Husband, Nox and the later hybrid books). She treats the versions of Sappho and Greek drama as part of the same imaginative world, not as the base of the claim. She concedes that some later books may be mannered.
responses.response: This answers the authorship question I raised in round 1 better than I expected. If the case is carried by the original books, translation and adaptation no longer narrow the claim, and I withdraw part of that objection. A properly scoped Carson citation is viable, and it is the strongest alternative to my own. What I still cannot resolve is the one you concede, that some later books may be mannered. It is also unsettled whether a body of work resting on a handful of titles carries the whole-oeuvre standard as firmly as a continuous project does. So my order stays the same, but the distance between the two cases is smaller than my round 1 ranking implied.

responses.point: Carlberg argues that in Carson's strongest books translation and original verse cannot be separated. Nox is plainly her own elegy, and Autobiography of Red reworks Stesichorus into new narrative. She prefers formal development across books to what she calls long-form repetition, and keeps Cărtărescu as her first alternative.
responses.response: I accept the point about Nox. An elegy built from a Catullus translation is original creation by any reasonable measure. I also accept that formal renewal from book to book is real evidence of sustained quality, and I do not dispute that Carson shows it. Your contrast with long-form repetition is the point I contest. Repetition has to be shown in the texts, and neither of us can show it from translation. I read the recurring motifs in Cărtărescu as one cosmology deepening, but that is a reading and not a demonstration. Where we differ is the weight given to continual change of form against a single vision pursued at scale. That is a difference of weighting, not of talent, and I do not think either weighting can be proved.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Cărtărescu first and says the late novels do not repeat the earlier books. She also says that the committee reads everything by shortlisted authors, and that unevenness should be tested and not assumed away.
responses.response: I agree that the late volumes must be read closely before a vote, and I welcome your insistence on it. I must keep separate what you assert and what I can confirm. In round 1 I said I could not verify from direct reading that the late novels develop and do not repeat, and that is still true. It supports the maturity claim only if it is checked. I would want the test to include the poetry and early work, where my coverage is thinner than for the major novels. If the committee cannot do that reading, I think we should say plainly that the maturity judgment on Cărtărescu rests on translation and reception, as the Carson judgment does.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Carson first and cites her classical learning and formal invention. He notes that her peak may lie in roughly 1998-2010, and that Cărtărescu's long digressive structures raise a question of economy and control that Carson's concentration avoids.
responses.response: The economy question is the right one and I do not claim Cărtărescu is economical. His achievement is a different kind, a sustained architecture whose digressions serve the larger design, and economy is not the measure that fits it. By the standard I stated above, the comparison is whether the voice develops. Your point about Carson's peak is useful, though I treat it as a member's unverified impression and not as a settled fact. A Carson citation drawn from the established core is sound on that reading. The same discipline applies to mine, which should rest on what is demonstrably central in the Cărtărescu corpus and not on the whole bulk. The remaining difference is whether concentration or scale better fits the whole-oeuvre standard.

responses.point: Palm ranks Carson first and weighs repeated invention of new forms more heavily than the scale of one vision. She does not hold the Romanian-translation gap against Cărtărescu, and treats it as an open limit on both judgements.
responses.response: I appreciate that you do not use the translation gap against Cărtărescu, and I would not use the Greek and Latin dependence against Carson either. The limit is the same for both. I agree range as well as intensity counts, and Carson shows range. The question is whether a long-pursued single vision that keeps changing in register, from the poetry to the novels, is also a form of development. I think it can be, but that is a view and not a proof. I also take your earlier question about 'ideal direction' as applying to both candidates equally. Neither is excused by genre or disqualified by it.

uncertainties: How much of Cărtărescu's achievement lies in Romanian syntax, rhythm and density that translations, and therefore my reading, carry only partly. I cannot confirm sentence-level quality directly.
Whether the late long novels develop or repeat earlier motifs. I have not verified this by close reading, and my knowledge of the poetry and early work is thinner than of the major novels.

Whether Carson's later books keep the level of the established core, and how much of her effect survives translation and standard editions given its dependence on layout and book design. I have not verified either point.

Whether the committee reads concentrated formal renewal (Carson, Michon) or large-scale imaginative construction in one voice (Cărtărescu) as better meeting the whole-oeuvre standard. I regard this as a difference of weighting and not one that can be settled by evidence.

The round 1 files give little developed argument for Adonis (B044) or Michon (B015), and my own coverage of both is limited. I ranked Michon third for compression and consistency. Whether intensity can offset the limits of a compact corpus is still undecided, and the sentence texture of his French is something I judge only through translation.
All assessments rest on general public knowledge and translations. No text or source was independently verified, and I do not claim to have read the full corpus of any shortlisted writer.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict requiring recusal is apparent from the supplied profile. It records no personal, professional or family tie to Cărtărescu, Carson, Michon, Adonis or any other shortlisted writer. I was elected to the Academy together with Ingrid Carlberg, which is an institutional fact and not a tie to a candidate. My own fiction and criticism on Central Europe, and my long residence in Prague and Vienna, are context only. Cărtărescu writes from the same wider region, and I disclose that adjacency without treating it as a connection or as evidence of preference. This disclosure is unchanged from round 1.
